snippet.description:
Take a look at 3 English language grammar rules to find out where they come from and if you actually need to follow them.

--

Grammatical rules have caused heated debate in various regions and languages for centuries. But while we know people take grammar seriously, what’s less clear is, why? Where do these seemingly random rules come from, and which, if any, actually matter? Arika Okrent takes a closer look at three famous examples from the English language that have been the source of numerous grammatical arguments.

Lesson by Arika Okrent, directed by Sharon Colman.

snippet.title: Weapon "Mass-Production" - The Last Roman Innovation That Saved the Empire
snippet.description:
Purchase "The Book" here for 10% off with our code "HISTORIAMILITUM10": https://mdsh.io/fcduk0y4zl

As the Late Roman army was hit by civil wars, invasions, and economic collapse, the old system of supplying the army was shattered. But in a surprising feat of resilience, the Empire evolved this system into something approaching modern mass-production. They created state-run factories in secure cities that secretly mass-producing everything the Late Empire's army needed, from plumbata darts and spathae. Along with this arsenal were more specialized weapons not seen by legionaries before, like clubs designed to crush Persian cataphracts at Singara and axes that pierced Gothic armor at Adrianople.

Was this truly mass production or just an exaggeration? This video explores the transition from small, self-reliant legionary forges to a centralized, state-controlled military-industrial network, and asks whether the Late Roman army's logistics were actually an upgrade from the Principate.

snippet.title: Every American Tank Sent to Russia in WW2 EXPLAINED
snippet.description:
Every American Tank Sent to Russia in WW2 EXPLAINED

Every American tank sent to Russia in WW2 explained — from the M3 Stuart light tank and M3 Lee medium tank to the M4A2 Sherman (75mm and 76mm). We are covering Lend-Lease deliveries, Eastern Front combat performance, Soviet crew nicknames like the "Emcha," and why the Red Army loved one American tank but despised the others.

The United States shipped over 6,500 tanks to the USSR under the Lend-Lease Act, including 1,676 M3 Stuarts, 1,386 M3 Lees, and 4,102 M4A2 Shermans. Delivered specifically for Soviet use, these diesel-powered machines fought from Operation Barbarossa through Kursk, Stalingrad, the Vistula-Oder Offensive, the Vienna Offensive, the Battle of Berlin, and finally Operation August Storm in Manchuria.

Soviet tankers called the M3 Lee "the grave for seven brothers" for its catastrophic fire risk and poor hull-mounted 75mm sponson traverse. Conversely, the M4A2 76mm Sherman earned elite assignments to Guards Mechanized Corps formations like the 9th Guards and 1st Mechanized Corps.

Whether you are a WW2 history enthusiast, a War Thunder or World of Tanks player grinding the Soviet or American tech tree, or a Hell Let Loose veteran who knows the Sherman's value, this breakdown covers every variant, production number, crew account, and combat action in full. The Emcha wasn't just a stopgap — it was a frontline weapon that helped drive the Red Army to final victory.

snippet.title: Pregnant at 13: The Girl Who Gave England a King
snippet.description:
She wasn’t a warrior queen. She didn’t sit on a throne or command armies. No — her story was far more fragile, and far more tragic.

At just thirteen years old, she was married off, her body barely grown, her life already mapped out by powerful men. Within a year she was pregnant — a child forced to bear a child. Yet from that ordeal came a son who would change England forever.

This wasn’t legend. This was the life of Lady Margaret Beaufort.

For centuries, dynasties rose and fell in England’s Wars of the Roses, but Margaret’s gamble secured the crown for her son, Henry Tudor — the boy who would return from exile to defeat Richard III at Bosworth and become Henry VII, founder of the Tudor dynasty. She endured loss, political betrayal, and the suffocating limits placed on medieval women, yet through cunning, faith, and unshakable will, she shaped the fate of a kingdom.

In this video, we uncover the story of a girl who should have been forgotten — but instead became the mother of a king, and the grandmother of Henry VIII.

Was it ambition? Was it survival? Or was it destiny that drove her?

This is the story of Lady Margaret Beaufort — the child bride who gave England a dynasty.

snippet.title: What causes avalanches, and can you survive them? - Simon Trautman
snippet.description:
Explore the three conditions needed to trigger an avalanche, and what makes these natural disasters so hard to survive.

--

Avalanches are the rapid descent of snow, ice, rock, or a combination of these down a slope. They can be destructive natural disasters and personal tragedies: killing an average of 27 people annually in the US. These alpine nightmares don’t just awaken out of nowhere; they need three specific conditions. So, what causes an avalanche? And is there any way to survive? Simon Trautman investigates.

snippet.title: The Immortals: Ancient Persia’s Most FEARED Elite Soldiers
snippet.description:
Most people know the Spartans — the red cloaks, the shields locked tight, the warriors who stood to the last man at Thermopylae. They’ve become the symbol of ancient discipline, courage, and defiance. But long before Sparta rose, another force dominated the world — an army so disciplined, so loyal, that their enemies believed they could never die.

They were called the Immortals — the elite guard of Ancient Persia’s Achaemenid Empire. Ten thousand strong, handpicked from the finest warriors of the Persian army, they fought under kings like Cyrus the Great, Cambyses II, and Darius I, guarding the empire that stretched from Egypt to India. Whenever one Immortal fell, another immediately took his place. Their number never changed. Their ranks never broke. To the world, they looked eternal — unstoppable — divine.

Clad in glittering scale armor, armed with spears tipped in gold and silver, and backed by the wealth of the largest empire on earth, the Persian Immortals were more than soldiers — they were living symbols of imperial power. They conquered Babylon, crushed rebellions, and stood at the heart of Persia’s greatest victories and defeats — from Babylon and Egypt to Thermopylae and Plataea.

But behind their splendor lay strategy, propaganda, and psychological warfare. Their very presence on the battlefield was meant to inspire awe — and fear. Even after their empire fell to Alexander the Great, the legend of the Immortals lived on, inspiring new armies from the Sasanian cavalry to Napoleon’s Imperial Guard and even modern Iran’s Javidan Guard.

This is the story of the 10,000 Immortals of Ancient Persia — the soldiers who turned fear into power, vanished with an empire, and yet never truly died.

Welcome to History Blends.

This wasn’t just a dethroned monarch meeting his end. This was a calculated execution, cloaked in secrecy and silence. A red-hot iron. A hollow horn. And a plan to murder a king… without leaving a single mark.

Edward II wasn’t the king his father wanted him to be. He was sensitive, artistic — and dangerously loyal to his favorites. First Piers Gaveston. Then Hugh Despenser. Their presence at court shattered alliances, enraged nobles, and brought his rule to ruin. But the betrayal that ended him didn’t come from an enemy. It came from his own wife — Queen Isabella — and her lover, Roger Mortimer.

What followed was a slow-motion collapse: defeat at Bannockburn, public humiliation, and finally, imprisonment in a castle built not to house royalty… but to erase them.

This is the story of a man born to rule, but not made for war. A king caught between personal love and political power. And a death so brutal, so grotesque, that it echoed across centuries.

Was it justice? Revenge? Or a royal cover-up?

snippet.title: Every US Tank Recovery Vehicle of WW2 Explained
snippet.description:
Every US Tank Recovery Vehicle of WW2 Explained

Every US Tank Recovery Vehicle of WW2 Explained — from the M31 TRV built on the phased-out M3 Lee chassis to the iconic M32 Sherman-based ARV, the M33 and M34 prime movers, and the legendary M25 Dragon Wagon tank transporter, this video breaks down every American armored recovery vehicle that kept US armor fighting across North Africa, Sicily, Italy, Normandy, the northwest European theater, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa. We cover the M31's 30-ton Gar Wood winch and 30,000-lb crane, the M32's 60,000-lb Garwood Special winch and 18-foot A-frame jib, production variants from Baldwin Locomotive Works, Lima Locomotive Works, Pressed Steel Car, and Pacific Car and Foundry, plus Lend-Lease deliveries to Britain and the Soviet Union. Whether you're tracking down the technical specs on the Hall-Scott 440-powered M26 tractor, comparing the M3A1, M3A3, and M4A1 hull variants, or fielding recovery vehicles in War Thunder or Steel Division, this is your complete breakdown of WWII US armored recovery and logistics. From the Tunisian campaign and Anzio minefield operations to the Dragon Wagon hauling Shermans and Pershings across Europe, we trace the full operational history of every vehicle in the US Army's WW2 tank recovery fleet.

snippet.title: Immersive Film | National Wallace Monument
snippet.description:
The National Wallace Monument is one of Scotland’s most iconic landmarks. It celebrated it's 150th anniversary with a complete refurbishment designed by Studio Arc. We were commissioned to create two central AVs for the new galleries located within the tower

A bespoke six metre screen and 5.1 surround sound immerses visitors in the powerful, emotional, and enduring story of Wallace's life, from his rise to prominence and victory at Stirling Bridge, to his elevation to national icon.

We worked with artist Richard Anderson to develop a distinct visual narrative and original illustrations with a bold, monochromatic style. Brush stroke effects drive camera movement. Ink spots representing water and blood emphasise the more violent aspects of the story. Additional layers of smoke, glare and particle effects create mood whilst adding depth.

The film has a dynamic, tension-building score by composer Giles Lamb. The script was developed by BBC Director Richard Downes and is recorded in eight languages.

snippet.title: The Hidden History of North Korea
snippet.description:
This story uncovers the enigmatic past of North Korea, a country known for its strict isolation and secretive regime. The narrative spans 15 chapters, each lasting 50-60 seconds, providing a comprehensive exploration of North Korea's transformation from an economic leader in East Asia to a tightly controlled state. The tale delves into unexpected historical truths, such as the unresolved Korean War and the rich legacy of the Korean Peninsula before the division. Presented in an accessible and engaging manner, this narrative avoids political controversies while revealing forgotten chapters of the nation’s past.

The story begins by painting a vivid picture of a prosperous Korea that once thrived as a unified economic power. The people enjoyed vibrant trade and cultural exchanges, but internal divisions and external pressures led to a dramatic transformation. As the story unfolds, the contrast between North Korea's past and present becomes apparent, with long-forgotten memories of bustling markets and creative industries clashing with the present-day isolation and control. Beneath the surface, whispers of a more complex reality persist, with personal struggles and quiet rebellions revealing the depth of the nation’s concealed history.

The climax unveils shocking truths about the ongoing Korean War, still unresolved since 1953. This revelation challenges common perceptions and forces a reevaluation of the region's history. Despite the government's strict control, moments of humor and rebellion emerge, offering brief escapes from the weight of secrecy. As the story reaches its conclusion, the tension between North Korea's past prosperity and its present isolation builds to a powerful revelation, leaving the audience questioning the future of this fractured nation.

snippet.title: New Unit Cohesion Mechanic for Total War: Medieval 3 (Idea)
snippet.description:
A new proposed "Unit Cohesion" mechanic for Total War: Medieval 3. With the War Core engine and the early development stage of the game, I figured it was time to open a discussion on how to improve historical combat for Total War. Link to presentation: https://miro.com/app/board/uXjVGTtlPgE=/?share_link_id=304447018859

The Problem:
Historical battles have stagnated due to low unit variety and limited paths to victory (always hammer and anvil). The binary nature of morale also means that nothing mechanically happens to a unit before it flees, leading to boring and grinding gameplay.

The Solution:
Introduce a new "unit cohesion" mechanic that fundamentally changes a unit's behavior prior to being routed to allow for more unit differentiation and tactical options.

The Definition:
"Unit Cohesion" is the degree to which individuals act as a unit. This is very important for historical accuracy where the armies were indeed made of individuals whose ability to win was dictated by the leader's ability to command and control them properly. In fact, most battles were won or lost based on this cohesion rather than casualties.

How it works:
Each unit will now have a Unit Leader that serves as the anchor of the unit and to which the other soldiers of that unit are magnetized to. The level of cohesion of a unit dictates how efficiently these soldiers follow the orders of the leader. So if you give an order, the leader goes first, followed by the rest of the men in a response time proportional to their cohesion. In terms of movement, cohesion degrades the farther and faster you go. When a unit stops moving, it can regain cohesion. For combat, a unit's cohesion dictates how effectively it can fight an opponent. More cohesion (and other factors) mean you can push other unit back. More cohesion mean you can withstand cavalry charges.  

Micro Cohesion:
We need an ability to customize units to improve their cohesion stats. This should include a way to select a unit leader and also a support staff (officers, musicians, bannermen) who can improve a unit's cohesion. There should be tools to visualize and test cohesion outside of actual battles such as a "Training Ground" mode.

Macro Cohesion:
A battle line now becomes much more fluid and dynamic as each unit's engagement ebbs and flows based on their cohesion. Generals and other abilities can help influence the state of cohesion of their forces. There should also be a cohesion system for unit's within larger formations. This could work like Carthay's Harmony system.

snippet.title: The Last Untouched Frontier Is About to Be Mined
snippet.description:
As Norway prepares for a historic vote, it could become the first country to open its waters to deep sea mining—unlocking vast mineral wealth beneath the Arctic seabed. 

But scientists warn the risks are unknown, ecosystems are fragile, and the consequences could be irreversible. 

From activists in Oslo to policymakers, industry leaders, and Pacific island nations weighing their own futures, this episode explores a global race for resources—and asks whether humanity is ready to mine the last untouched frontier on Earth.
